questions.question: What does ColBERT store for each document?
options: One vector per token, computed offline
A single vector for the whole document
One scalar weight per vocabulary term
A joint query-document pair encoding

questions.topic: Late Interaction: ColBERT Token-Level Matching and PLAID Serving
questions.question: How does ColBERT score a query against a document?
options: Cosine between the two [CLS] vectors
Dot product of sparse vocabulary vectors
Sum over query tokens of each token's best document-token match
A linear layer over the concatenated pair encoding

questions.topic: Late Interaction: ColBERT Token-Level Matching and PLAID Serving
questions.question: Why is ColBERT described as late interaction?
options: It reranks only after BM25 has finished
Query and document are encoded independently and interact only in final scoring
It delays all indexing until the first query arrives
Its training happens after the cross-encoder trains

questions.topic: Late Interaction: ColBERT Token-Level Matching and PLAID Serving
questions.question: A 200-token document stored at 128 dimensions per token in 2-byte values costs about how much space?
options: About 1.5 KB
About 6 KB
About 13 KB
About 51 KB

questions.topic: Late Interaction: ColBERT Token-Level Matching and PLAID Serving
questions.question: How does PLAID make ColBERT serving fast at corpus scale?
options: It converts token vectors into BM25 weights
It caches top results for repeated queries
It recalls candidates through centroids, then applies full MaxSim only to a shortlist
It replaces MaxSim with one document-level dot product

questions.topic: Late Interaction: ColBERT Token-Level Matching and PLAID Serving
questions.question: Which team should prefer ColBERT over single-vector dense retrieval?
options: One wanting token-level match explainability that can afford much larger indexes
One needing the smallest possible index footprint
One with no accelerator available at ingest time
One whose queries never repeat any vocabulary

questions.question: What is the training signal in cross-encoder distillation?
options: Human thumbs-up feedback from production logs
The teacher model's scores on query-document pairs
The student model's own previous checkpoints
Random labels balanced across relevance classes

questions.question: Why do soft teacher scores teach better than hard relevance labels?
options: They require fewer training queries overall
They remove the need for a validation set
They are cheaper to store on disk
They encode graded distinctions between nearly-relevant negatives

questions.question: Why does distillation make economic sense for serving?
options: Expensive teacher compute happens once offline while the cheap student serves indefinitely
The teacher model becomes free after training
The student needs no evaluation pass afterward
Distillation removes the index rebuild cycle

questions.question: How can a team adapt its ranker to a new domain with no human relevance judgments?
options: Train the teacher on random domain pairs
Skip adaptation, since bi-encoders are domain-free
Distill the teacher's scores on unlabeled domain queries into the student
Fine-tune the student on synthetic labels from BM25 alone

questions.question: A distilled bi-encoder reproduces its teacher's blind spot on product codes. Why does this happen?
options: The student has too many parameters
Product codes change too frequently for indexing
The index was built with the wrong metric
The teacher's systematic errors became the student's training targets

questions.question: Why is distilling a distilled model into an even smaller one usually a mistake?
options: Small models cannot consume soft labels
Each generation compounds approximation error and the capacity gap
Grand-student models require far more training data
The original teacher's license forbids it
